extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, or critical reasoning (readers evaluating arguments and generalizations)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the validity of generalizations, inductions, analogies, and classifications in argumentation. Emphasizes distinguishing empirical from causal laws, avoiding common fallacies (simple enumeration, post hoc, false analogies), and ensuring proper classification and explanatory depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize irreducible distinctions between types of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Where consciousness recognizes an inherent distinction between two phenomena (e.g., motion and sensation), attempts to reduce one under the laws of the other are false; one may be a cause or condition of the other, but not identical with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate different logical kinds (qualitative vs. mechanistic accounts). Even if a sequence of physical causes leads to a sensation, the final sensation is not merely another motion; explanations must respect category-differences. Avoid theories that pretend to subsume qualitatively distinct phenomena under a single type without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simple enumeration (enumeratio simplex) as induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction by mere enumeration — observing instances A1, A2, A3 are B and concluding all A are B — is a rude and slovenly mode of generalization and is provisional at best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require elimination and exclusion of counter-instances rather than relying on what is 'readily at hand'. Use comparisons and ascertain material facts; avoid accepting common-sense maxims that rest on mere absence of counterexamples (e.g., 'whatsoever has never been, will never be'). Treat such generalizations as empirical, limited by the bounds of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer impossibility from non-observation
rubrics_metrics.description: A phenomenon never having been noticed only proves the required conditions have not yet occurred in experience; it does not prove it cannot occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially wary of negative generalizations (negations) as they form the weakest empirical laws. Prefer empirical laws that display gradations and regularities enabling rational extrapolation rather than absolute negations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer empirical laws with gradation/series for extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: When observations present a series with gradations and apparent regularity (a mathematical-like law), one may rationally presume about terms beyond observation; this is a higher kind of empirical law than mere negation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for continuous series, gradations, or mathematical regularities in data before extrapolating. Use such structure to justify limited inferences beyond the observed range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical (customary) laws from causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws express customary order of succession of effects but are not ultimate; causal laws identify the determinate causes producing phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating empirical regularities as ultimate explanations. Investigate underlying causes that produce observed empirical patterns; only when causes are ascertained can one claim a genuine law of causation and make stronger predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generalizing from one time/place to all times/places without cause-based justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations from present to past or from one society to another often err when they assume conditions constant across time or place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take current local or temporal states as universal types. When extrapolating, examine whether the same causal conditions hold in the target time/place; otherwise restrict conclusions to 'adjacent cases' where conditions are similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer causation from mere temporal or conjunctive conjunction (post hoc/cum hoc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring that A caused B because A preceded or co-occurred with B (post hoc, cum hoc) is a vulgar fallacy unless other evidence supports causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require elimination of alternative antecedents and look for presumption from known properties of the supposed agent. Use additional evidence or mechanisms that would plausibly connect A to B rather than relying solely on sequence or conjunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false theory / oversimplified single-cause explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad generalization a priori (false theory) arises from deducing conclusions solely from properties of one agent while overlooking other coexisting agents and causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist attempts to explain complicated phenomena by a simpler theory than warranted (e.g., attributing all disease to one bodily condition). Consider multiple interacting causes and test whether the hypothesized single cause has sufficient explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat analogical arguments as weak unless causal connection shown
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument from analogy (inferring B for case 2 because case 1 has A and B and case 2 has A) affords only a small increase in probability unless a causal link between A and B can be demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overrate the probative force of analogy. Where possible, show that A is one of the conditions that can produce B, or demonstrate a causal or lawlike connection; otherwise treat analogy as merely suggestive. Be explicit about how much additional probability the analogy provides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false analogies: do not infer resemblance in one respect from resemblance in another when evidence disconnects them
rubrics_metrics.description: False analogy occurs when resemblance in one property is used to infer resemblance in another materially distinct property, especially where evidence tends to disconnect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the supposed common property is relevant (i.e., causally connected) to the inferred property. Provide justification that the same law operates in both cases rather than relying on superficial resemblance. Examples include faulty analogies from family government to state despotism or from bodies natural to bodies politic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphors/figures of speech only to illustrate, not to prove
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors and analogies aid apprehension and can suggest directions for proof but do not constitute proof themselves; their applicability must be shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a metaphor is used, make explicit the parity (similarity of relations) it rests upon and demonstrate how the metaphorical case shares the relevant causal relations. Avoid treating vivid metaphor as substitute for evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bad classification: ensure groupings share common important properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of generalization often arise from grouping together things that lack common properties (or share only trivial ones), producing misleading general propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define terms precisely and ensure class-membership rests on substantial shared properties relevant to the proposition being advanced. Beware of extending common-use words to heterogeneous cases without verification (e.g., broad medieval concepts like 'humidum' or loose uses of 'motion' to denote all change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against ambiguity and conflation of meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Using words that are extended or vague in meaning (e.g., motion used to mean all change) produces confusion and undermines sound reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify senses of key terms before argumentation. When a single term covers heterogeneous phenomena, either restrict its meaning or subdivide into distinct concepts to avoid fallacious inferences.
